# Introduction

This is an R markdown document. In R Studio, you can also generate another kind 
of markdown file called an R notebook. The notebook allows you to preview your
work as you go in the viewer. This can also be achieved, however, by checking
"Knit on Save" when building a standard markdown. Both approaches are excellent
for report development and for learning.

In this workshop, we'll cover the basics of R markdown and how to use it to 
build automated reports. We'll cover:

- R markdown file format 

- Code chunk settings 

    - Output formatting 

    - Figure display 

    - Conditional execution 

- Narrative options 

    - Embedded links 

    - Dynamic text 

    - Custom styling with CSS 

- Parameters 

    - Automated report running 

    - Rendering via a script  

    - Error handling frameworks  

- Useful packages for R markdown reports 

Before we move on, take a look to the right side of the source pane and you'll
notice the Outline in a separate scrollable box. The Outline allows you to jump
to named sections and code chunks in your file. Sections are created with "#",
and code chunks are named following "```{r " in the chunk header. If you don't
see the Outline, click Tools > Global Options > R Markdown > Basic and check
"Show document outline by default". 

# R Markdown Format

R Markdown files are specially formatted files that can be easily "rendered" to
HTML files. This makes them a flexible option for quickly converting code and
notes into reports. Unlike R scripts, R markdown files default to text. Unless 
the user creates a “code chunk”, anything written in the file (outside of YAML 
header) will be interpreted as simple text. Several text styling options are 
available in the default R markdown file; we’ll cover these later. This section 
and the Introduction above are narrative. 

Data analyses and visualizations are incorporated via code chunks, which are 
segments of the document specially formatted to interpret written text as R 
code. Code chunks have adjustable settings that can be globally and individually 
set for your document. We'll get into code chunks below.

# Code Chunk Settings

```{r setup}
# setting chunk options for my entire document 
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

```{r load_packages}

# To ensure the document can be "Knitted" for a preview, packages must be
# loaded in the document itself. If a document is rendered by a call in a 
# separate script, packages can be loaded elsewhere 

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(readxl)
library(flextable)
```

## Chunk Arguments for Text Output 

Here we'll demonstrate a few of the code chunk options available in markdown:

### Message

The `message` argument sets whether to display message outputs in rendered file 
from functions executed in code. Messages are generated by functions
to alert users to certain processes.

```{r message_fx, message = FALSE}
# Custom function that sends a message 
count <- c(1,2,3)
send_message <- function(vector) {
  for (i in seq_along(vector)) {
    # count down!
    message(i, " Mississippi!")
  }
}
```

```{r message_T, message = T}
# message prints out separately 
send_message(count)
```

```{r message_F, message = F}
# keeps message from this function hidden
send_message(count)
```

### Error & Warning

The `error` argument sets whether to continue rendering if an error is 
encountered (FALSE by default), and the `warning` argument sets whether to display 
warning outputs in rendered file from functions executed in code 
(TRUE by default). 

```{r err, error = T, warning = T}

# this will throw an error that prevents complete rendering of the file
# unless error = T
sum(c(1, 2, "3"))

# this will only print if the error is "ignored"
print("Nothing to see here, folks!")

```

```{r warn_show, warning = T}
# this function produces a warning message that NAs were imputed
# for all values where coercion to numeric was not possible
as.numeric(c("1", "2", "three"))
```

```{r warn_hide, warning = F}
# warning = F will hide the warning in the output
as.numeric(c("1", "2", "three"))
```

### Include

The `include` argument sets whether to display chunk results and the chunk itself 
in output document (TRUE by default). So far, we've chosen to display all our 
text outputs, but this argument makes it easy to obscure them.

```{r not_included, include = F}
# a covert message
print("No one will see this!")
```

### Results

The `results` argument has two settings, "markup", where text is displayed in
boxes (see all the outputs above), and "asis" where text output is converted 
to plain text.

In combination with the cat() function, this argument allows for narrative/HTML 
sections to be dynamically included in the output. 

```{r res_box, results = "markup"}
print("help, I'm stuck in this box!")
```

```{r res_print, results = "asis"}
# present text output as a narrative line
print("Ah, much better.")

# use cat() for even cleaner text
cat("Now I can do anything!!")
```

## Chunk Evaluation

You can choose whether or not to actually execute a code chunk by setting the 
`eval` argument, which takes a Boolean operator. Hard coding this operator is
useful during development, but setting it dynamically can really come in handy 
when rendering automated reports.

```{r dynamic_val}
# say we only want a certain chunk to evaluate if a certain user
# is running it

# Hey user, what's your name??
my_name <- "Sam"

# set the value 
if (my_name == "Sam") {
  name_val <- T
} else {
  name_val <- F
}
```

```{r sam_chunk, eval = name_val, results = "asis", echo = F}
# a message for Sam's report only
cat("Hey Sam, don't forget to save the report to the correct folder!")
```

## Chunk Arguments for Figures and Plots 

There are many ways to format figures and plots in reports. It can be very
convenient to apply certain formatting choices directly in the chunk settings,
though more complex formatting must be achieved through other means.

### Embedding Figures

Pre-saved images can be included in outputs via calls in code chunks. 
You can also use chunk arguments to provide captions and labels. 

```{r show_fig, fig.cap = "The cat is just doing his best"}
# if the image is not in the working directory, be sure to provide the full path
knitr::include_graphics('ok_cat.jpg')
```

### Resizing and Placing Figures

It's also possible to control image size and alignment via chunk arguments.You
can call `out.height` and `out.width` to specify the size of the image. These 
arguments work with saved images, and will not be affected by the similarly 
named `fig.height`, `fig.width`, and `fig.dim`, which work only when calling R 
objects (such as a ggplot). These arguments interpret the value input in inches. 

The `fig.align` argument allows you to quickly re-position the image, which can
be helpful for aesthetics of your report. There are more ways to adjust figure
size and position, and we'll address some of these later on.

```{r show_fig_wide, fig.cap = "Now the cat is flat", out.width = "700px", out.height = "20px"}
# when using out.height and out.width, you can use either the percent of 
# available space you'd like the image to take up or a specific measurement
# such as pixels
knitr::include_graphics('ok_cat.jpg')
```

```{r show_fig_right, fig.cap = "Now the cat is right", out.width = "200px", fig.align = 'right'}
# fig.align works with saved images and R objects alike!
knitr::include_graphics('ok_cat.jpg')
```

# Narrative Options

## Type Face Adjustments and Paragraphs

Markdown files understand certain cues in normal text that will change the 
face of the text. Here we'll also bring attention the easily applied paragraph
delineations, which have been used throughout this document thus far. Pressing
enter will send your text to a new line, but pressing it twice will start a new
paragraph, as shown below. 

Bold text can be achieved with **double asterisks**, or alternatively with
__double underscores__.

Italics can be applied with *single asterisks* and _single underscores_.

You can also simultaneously apply both with ***triple asterisks*** or
___underscores___. 

Generally speaking, asterisks behave more stably than underlines, and can even
be used to just change part of a word, like t**hi**s, whereas the underscores
don't work in t__hi__s case. 

It is also possible to force markdown to interpret these characters simply,
and not as type face adjustments. To do this, we need to use an
"escape character". In R markdown, the escape character is the backslash. Here,
I can "escape" the effect of my \*asterisks\* to keep the font face normal and
show the asterisks themselves. 

## Embedding Links, Dynamic Text, and Figures 

Adding links to your text is very easy. Simply type the visible text within
square brackets immediately followed by the link in parentheses. If I want to
direct viewers to a brief overview of the cat meme I used above, I'd link to
it [here](https://en.meming.world/wiki/Thumbs_Up_Crying_Cat). 

It's also common to want to include text that changes based on input parameters
or the outcome of functions called in code chunks. You can do this by calling 
objects "inline", where markdown will interpret them as if they are in code
chunks. Earlier, I set the object `my_name`, I can interpret it dynamically by
using back ticks and a lower case r:

"Hi, my name is `r my_name`. Nice to meet you!"

You can also write new code to be evaluated in these inline chunks, though it's
best to keep these calls brief. A great example is using the inline to dynamically
write today's date.

Today's date is `r format(Sys.Date(), format = "%B %d, %Y")`.

Finally, while it's preferable to add figures in other ways, it is possible to
embed figures in text by using the link format preceded by an exclamation mark.
Here's a different cat: ![table cat](cat_table.jpg).

## Lists, Block Quotes, and Horizontal Rules

Adding bullets and lists to markdown is fairly simple:

1. Press enter twice to start a new paragraph
2. Type "1." to start your numbered list
3. Repeat as necessary
    a. Simply indent **twice** and type sub-items as you'd like them to appear
  
- Bullets can be added using dashes
- You can also use "+" or "*" but it's best to pick a character and stick to it!

Block quotes can be added using the right arrow character, ">". Let's say I want
to quote the article I linked above. I'd do it by starting a new paragraph, 
indenting once, and using the arrow:

  > "The “Thumbs Up Crying Cat” meme is a reaction image involving the photoshopped image of a cat giving the viewer a thumbs-up gesture. This sister image to "Crying Cat" has commonly been used to indicate a mixture of sadness but acceptance of a situation, possibly to avoid being difficult."
    
To end this section with a nice horizontal rule, I'll simply type three lone
underscores in a new paragraph.

___

## Custom Styling with CSS

For the most precise control over fonts, text appearance, and arrangement of
elements in a document, you can use a .css file to "style" your markdown. The
CSS file will contain specially formatted instructions which you can then call
in your markdown file to apply. Creating a new CSS file in R is as easy as
clicking File > New file > CSS File. Once created, save it with a name and then
link your markdown to the CSS in the YAML header.

In the following sections I'll show how CSS can be incorporated to achieve great
visual results. There are several ways to do this, but my team likes to use 
"div" elements and grid layouts to create products. When using "div" 
elements, you have more control, but that also means fewer things happen
automatically. Headings, for example need to be "styled" and then called with
the "class" argument in the div opener:

<div class="header-text">
Here's My CSS Styled Heading
</div>

<div class="body-text-italics">
CSS is great for applying styling options to a whole section of text. Rather
than wrapping all of this in asterisks, I applied my custom CSS style. Also, 
within div elements we do still need to use escape characters to simply type
\*\*special characters\*\*.
</div>

<div class="body-text-normal", style="text-align: center;">
You can also have set styles that you tweak with calls to arguments in the div 
opener. For this chunk I used my base text style and then added center alignment
in the opener via the "style" argument. 
</div>
    
<div class="body-text-normal">
With CSS and the grid layout, we can design page layouts with "containers" and
use these to arrange blocks of text or images on the page. The container will
be the outermost div element, and the objects within the container will be in
nested div elements. See how this looks below.
</div>

<div class="container-1">
<div class="contain1-a">
<div class="purple-quote">
"One cat just leads to another"

\- Ernest Hemingway
</div>
</div>
<div class="contain1-b", style="border: 4px solid #6A5ACD; padding: 5px; border-radius: 10px;">
```{r the_third_cat, echo = F}
knitr::include_graphics('suspicious_cat.jpg')
```
</div>
</div>

<div class="body-text-normal">
Total customization via CSS is great, but specifying everything can be very 
time-consuming. R markdown documents use Bootstrap styling by default, and thus 
can have a number of pre-built "Bootswatch themes" applied to them. The `bslib`
package gives you access to the widest range of standard and modern [Bootswatch
themes](https://bootswatch.com/). 
</div>

```{r load_bookdown, echo = F}
library(bookdown)
```

<div class="body-text-normal">
Finally, if the desired output format is simply HTML, then you do not need to
worry about pagination. However, if the desired output of your document is PDF, pagination is key. My team uses the `pagedown` package to handle paging and HTML to PDF conversion.
</div>

<div class="body-text-normal">
If you do not specify page breaks in your markdown file and convert the
rendered HTML to PDF, breaks will automatically insert as pages fill up. This
can be aesthetically pleasing by chance, but if the goal is to create an
automated report with predictable formatting and page content, then setting
page breaks is a *must*. I do this below by typing backslash pagebreak:
</div>

\pagebreak

<div class="page-header">
<div class="header-textbox" style="float:left; width:70%;">
<div class="header-text">Here's a custom header</div>
<div class="header-subtext">Hello there `r my_name`!</div>
</div>
</div>

```{r penguin_plot_fx, echo = F, eval = F}

# use eval = F when previewing this notebook in the viewer or if you want
# to exclude the penguin plot when rendering to HTML

penguin_plot = function(data, name) {
  
  if (name == "Haley") {
    data <- data %>% filter(species %in% c("Adelie", "Gentoo"))
  } else if(name == "Paul") {
    data <- data %>% filter(species %in% c("Gentoo", "Chinstrap"))
  } else if(name == "Sam") {
    data <- data %>% filter(species %in% c("Adelie", "Chinstrap"))
  } else {
    # if your name is not on the list, no data for you!
    data <- data %>% filter(species == "none") %>% select(-bill_length_mm)
  }
  
  # build simple ggplot
  plot <- ggplot(data) +
    geom_boxplot(mapping = aes(x = species, y = bill_length_mm, 
                               fill = species)) +
    labs(x = "", y = "Bill Length (mm)",
         title = paste0("Penguin Plot for ", name), fill = "Species") +
    theme_classic()
  
  # save it as a png
  ggsave(plot, filename = "penguin_plot.png",
         width = 4, height = 2.75, units = "in")
}

```

```{r plot_penguins, echo = F, warning = F, eval = F}

# use eval = F when previewing this notebook in the viewer or if you want
# to exclude the penguin plot when rendering to HTML

# run custom function
penguin_plot(penguins, my_name2)
knitr::include_graphics("penguin_plot.png")
```

# Useful Packages for Markdown Reports

Here I'll use the `flextable` package to create a nice table of useful packages
for writing attractive HTML reports in markdown. This is by no means an
exhaustive list, but my team returns to these packages time and time again when
building data products.

```{r package_tbl, echo = F}

# load in table
packs <- read_xlsx("useful_packages_R.xlsx")

# format with flextable
packs_tbl <- flextable(packs) %>%
  # table title/header
  add_header_row(values = c("Useful Packages for Markdown Reports"),
                 colwidths = c(4)) %>%
  bold(bold = TRUE, part = "header") %>%
  # set column widths
  width(j = 1:4, width = 1.5, unit = "in") %>%
  # merge cells in intermediate spanner rows
  # this is a funky but functional way to make spanners
  merge_h() %>%
  # cell background color, i = rows, j = cols
  bg(i = 1, 
     bg = "#9dd0fa", part = "body") %>%
  bg(i = 2:5, 
     bg = "#c7e4fc", part = "body") %>%
  bg(i = 6, 
     bg = "#89f781", part = "body") %>%
  bg(i = 7:10, 
     bg = "#c6fcc2", part = "body") %>%
  bg(i = 11, 
     bg = "#f5f264", part = "body") %>%
  bg(i = 12:13, 
     bg = "#faf9ac", part = "body") %>%
  bg(i = 14, 
     bg = "#f58771", part = "body") %>%
  bg(i = 15:17, 
     bg = "#fac6bb", part = "body")

```

```{r render_tbl, echo = F}
packs_tbl
```
